question.prompt: Why did the authors want to replace recurrent networks in sequence models?

options.text: Because recurrent models process positions one by one, blocking parallel computation within an example
Because recurrent networks cannot be combined with attention at all
Because convolutional networks always beat recurrent networks on translation

sourceRefs.quote: This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths

concepts.explanation: Recurrent networks compute hidden states step by step, so each step has to wait for the previous one to finish. That sequential dependency makes it hard to parallelize training, especially as sentences get longer, which was the core motivation for a different architecture.
concepts.simpler: RNNs read a sentence one word at a time in order, so you can't speed them up much by doing things in parallel.
concepts.example: A made-up example: translating a 50-word sentence with an RNN means waiting through 50 sequential steps, like reading a book one page at a time even if you have many readers available.

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Let's look closer at how recurrent networks actually compute, step by step.

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: They generate a hidden state for each position, but each one needs the state right before it.

sourceRefs.quote: they generate a sequence of hidden states ht, as a function of the previous hidden state ht−1 and the input for position t

beats.speaker: player
beats.text: So step five can't start until step four is done?

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Exactly. Slow down with me here: that chain means no shortcuts, no skipping ahead.

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: This sequential nature blocks parallel work within a single training example.

sourceRefs.quote: This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: It's a bit like a bucket brigade: each person must wait for the bucket before passing it on.

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: And the problem grows with longer sentences, since memory limits how much you can batch instead.

sourceRefs.quote: which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Quick check before we move on.

check.prompt: According to Table 1, how many sequential operations does a recurrent layer need?

options.text: A constant number, O(1)
A number that grows with sequence length, O(n)
A number that shrinks as sequences get longer

check.right: Right. Recurrence scales with sequence length, which is exactly the bottleneck.
check.wrong: Not quite. Table 1 shows recurrent layers need O(n) sequential steps, growing with sentence length.

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: So take this with you: recurrence forces waiting, and waiting is what blocks parallel training.

sourceRefs.quote: The fundamental constraint of sequential computation, however, remains

question.prompt: What is the purpose of using multiple attention heads instead of just one?

options.text: To let the model jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions
To make the total computation cheaper than single-head attention
To remove the need for positional encodings in the model

sourceRefs.quote: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.

concepts.explanation: A single attention head averages information across positions, which can blur useful distinctions. Running several smaller attention operations in parallel, each with its own learned projections, lets the model look at different kinds of relationships at once, then combine the results.
concepts.simpler: Instead of one big spotlight, the model uses several smaller spotlights that can each focus on a different kind of relationship in the sentence.
concepts.example: A made-up example: one head might track subject-verb agreement while another tracks which pronoun refers to which noun, and multi-head attention lets both happen simultaneously.

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Let's slow down on how multi-head attention actually works.

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: A single attention operation averages over positions. That averaging can wash out useful detail.

sourceRefs.quote: an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention as described in section 3.2

beats.speaker: player
beats.text: So one head just isn't enough?

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Right. With one head, averaging inhibits the model from separating different relationships.

sourceRefs.quote: With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this.

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: So instead, the queries, keys, and values get projected several times, each with its own learned projection.

sourceRefs.quote: we found it beneficial to linearly project the queries, keys and values h times with different, learned linear projections

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Think of it like reading a sentence with several different highlighters at once, each tracking its own kind of connection.

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Each projected version runs attention in parallel, then all the outputs get concatenated and projected once more.

sourceRefs.quote: These are concatenated and once again projected, resulting in the final values

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: That's why heads end up specializing. Figures show different heads tracking different things, like long-distance dependencies or anaphora.

sourceRefs.quote: Many of the attention heads attend to a distant dependency of the verb ‘making’

beats.speaker: player
beats.text: So each head notices something different, then it all gets combined.

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Exactly. Multiple heads let the model attend jointly to different representation subspaces, instead of blurring everything into one average.

sourceRefs.quote: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.

question.prompt: How did the Transformer perform on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task?

options.text: It reached 28.4 BLEU, beating the previous best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU
It tied with previous ensemble models but didn't surpass them
It set a new state of the art only on English-to-French, not English-to-German

sourceRefs.quote: Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English- to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU.

concepts.explanation: The Transformer didn't just match prior systems, it clearly outperformed them, including systems that combined multiple models together (ensembles). This result mattered because it showed the attention-only approach wasn't just faster, it was also more accurate.
concepts.simpler: The new model's translations scored noticeably better than even the best older systems, even ones using teams of models at once.
concepts.example: A made-up comparison: think of a race where the old champions were teams of runners, and a single new runner still crossed the line clearly ahead.

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Let's look at how this model actually did on translation.

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: On English-to-German, it hit a new best score, and not by a small margin.

sourceRefs.quote: Transformer (big) 28.4

beats.speaker: player
beats.text: Better than everything before it?

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Yes. It beat the best prior models, even ones that combined several models together.

sourceRefs.quote: outperforms the best previously reported models (including ensembles) by more than 2.0 BLEU

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: An aside: ensembles are like asking five experts and averaging their answers. Usually that wins.

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Here, one single attention-based model still came out ahead.

sourceRefs.quote: ConvS2S Ensemble [9] 26.36

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Quick check before we move on.

check.prompt: Even the smaller base model, compared to all prior models and ensembles, did what?

options.text: Matched them, but trained much faster
Surpassed them, at a fraction of the training cost
Fell slightly short but was simpler

check.right: Exactly. Even the lighter base model came out on top, and cheaply.
check.wrong: Not quite. The passage says the base model surpassed every prior model and ensemble too, at a fraction of the cost.

beats.speaker: player
beats.text: So speed wasn't the only win here.

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Right. The takeaway: this wasn't just a faster way to translate. It was a genuinely more accurate one.

sourceRefs.quote: establishing a new state-of-the-art BLEU score of 28.4

question.prompt: What trade-off happens if self-attention is restricted to a local neighborhood for long sequences?

options.text: The maximum path length between distant positions grows to O(n/r)
It removes the need for multiple attention heads entirely
It makes self-attention slower than recurrent layers no matter the sequence length

sourceRefs.quote: This would increase the maximum path length to O(n/r).

concepts.explanation: Full self-attention connects every position to every other position in one step, which is great for learning long-range dependencies but expensive for very long sequences. Restricting attention to a nearby window saves computation, but it brings back longer paths between distant words, which is exactly the problem self-attention was meant to avoid.
concepts.simpler: Looking only at nearby words saves work, but then far-apart words take more steps to connect again, which was the original problem attention solved.
concepts.example: A made-up example: if a pronoun at the end of a long paragraph refers to a name at the start, a narrow attention window might force the model to relay that connection through several intermediate steps instead of linking them directly.

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Full self-attention connects every position to every other position, all at once.

sourceRefs.quote: a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: That is exactly why it is so good at catching long-range dependencies.

sourceRefs.quote: The shorter these paths between any combination of positions in the input and output sequences, the easier it is to learn long-range dependencies

beats.speaker: player
beats.text: So why would anyone want less of that?

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Because for very long sequences, connecting everything to everything gets expensive.

sourceRefs.quote: To improve computational performance for tasks involving very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size r

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: So one idea is to only let each position look at a nearby window, size r, instead of the whole sequence.

sourceRefs.quote: self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size r in the input sequence centered around the respective output position

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Let me slow down here, because this is the catch. Restricting the window brings back a cost self-attention was built to avoid.

sourceRefs.quote: Self-Attention (restricted) O(r · n · d) O(1) O(n/r)

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Two far-apart words now need several hops through the window to reach each other, instead of one direct step.

sourceRefs.quote: This would increase the maximum path length to O(n/r)

beats.speaker: player
beats.text: So it is a straight swap: speed for distance.

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Quick check before we move on.

check.prompt: What does restricting attention to a local window trade away?

options.text: It makes training sequential instead of parallel
It lengthens the path between distant positions again
It removes the need for positional encoding

check.right: Exactly. The constant path length full attention gave you stretches back out.
check.wrong: Not quite. The window stays parallel; what grows back is the path length between far positions.

beats.speaker: explainer
beats.text: Take away: local windows save computation, but they undo the very thing self-attention was prized for, short paths between any two positions.

sourceRefs.quote: In the Transformer this is reduced to a constant number of operations
